vignette:
The Weight of the Machine

Marcus is nineteen years old and works as a peer support counselor at a youth wellness center, a role he took partly because he genuinely wants to help people and partly, he admits quietly, because understanding other people's pain felt safer than sitting alone with his own. He is in a relationship with a young woman named Ellie, who he describes as patient and warm, and who has watched him change in ways neither of them fully understands yet.

Fourteen months ago, Marcus collapsed during a morning run. He was seventeen at the time, fit, with no history of anything serious, and the collapse seemed impossible in the way that only the most real things do. What followed was a week in the intensive care unit, a diagnosis of viral myocarditis — an inflammation of the heart muscle — and several days during which the doctors spoke carefully to his parents in hallways while Marcus lay connected to monitors, listening to the rhythmic beeping that told him his heart was still deciding. There was one night in particular when the arrhythmias worsened and a crash cart was brought to the door of his room. He did not lose consciousness. He remembers every second of it.

He recovered. His cardiologist now calls him a success story. Marcus nods when people say this, because he does not know how to explain that surviving and being okay are not the same thing.

The beeping follows him. Not literally — he knows that — but any electronic sound with a regular pulse, a microwave, a truck reversing, a notification tone on someone's phone, pulls him back to that room with a force that is almost physical. His chest tightens. His vision narrows. For a few seconds he is seventeen again and the crash cart is at the door. At the youth center, when a colleague's phone alarm goes off during a group session, Marcus has to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he grips the sink and talks himself back into his own body. He has become skilled at this, and skilled at making it invisible.

He sleeps badly. When he does sleep, he often wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart pounding, certain something is wrong with it, pressing his fingers to his wrist to count his pulse the way the nurses taught him. He has checked his pulse hundreds of times since leaving the hospital. He knows this is excessive. He cannot stop.

During the day he moves through a strange, muffled version of the world. He describes it as watching life through glass — present enough to function, distant enough to feel like a passenger in his own experience. He laughs at the right moments in conversation, offers genuine insight to the young people he counsels, and then drives home feeling hollowed out. Ellie tells him she misses him even when he is sitting right beside her, and he does not argue, because he understands exactly what she means.

What disturbs Marcus most, and what he has told almost no one, is that he no longer fully believes his body is safe. He was healthy and then he was dying and there was no warning and no reason. The logic of that sits inside him like a splinter. He exercises less now, afraid of what his heart might do. He avoids caffeine, avoids stress, avoids anything that makes his pulse rise — which means avoiding joy as much as fear, because his body cannot seem to tell the difference anymore.

He chose counseling because he wanted to be useful. He sits across from teenagers who are struggling and he listens with a quality of attention that his supervisor calls remarkable. What his supervisor does not know is that Marcus listens so carefully because he is also, always, listening to himself — waiting for the sound that means the machine inside his chest has decided, again, that it is done.
